title: Intermediate forms and parent species tend to go extinct

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Intermediate forms and parent species tend to go extinct

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: In a fully stocked country, improved descendants of a species tend to supplant their predecessors, so the intermediate forms between earlier and later states, and the original parent species itself, generally tend to become extinct.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Hence all the intermediate forms between the earlier and later states, that is between the less and more improved state of a species, as well as the original parent-species itself, will generally tend to become extinct.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter IV, “Natural Selection”; section “Action of Natural Selection, through Divergence of Character and Extinction, on the descendants from a common parent”. Scope: lineages of species descended from a common parent

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch04-23: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.58

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Fossil time series can test selected well-preserved lineages. The mechanism and universal tendency are difficult to distinguish from sampling loss and environmental extinction.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Reconstruct densely sampled fossil and extant lineages and test whether ancestral and morphologically intermediate forms disappear as derived descendants diversify. Temporal overlap followed by decline of ancestors and intermediates supports the prediction; persistent ancestor-descendant coexistence weakens it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Ancestors are rarely identifiable with confidence from sampled fossils.

Missing intermediates and last appearances are strongly affected by preservation.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.73
data adequacy: 0.5
analysis feasibility: 0.57
discriminating power: 0.43
operationalizability: 0.62

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The fate of intermediate forms is testable only where fossils, characters, and trees coincide, which is a small and biased slice of lineages. Identifying the parent species is itself theory-laden, so a result can be partly circular. Public databases support case-wise and clade-wise proxies, not a general count of ancestral extinction.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Along fossil lineages with phylogenetic trees, score whether morphologically intermediate forms and putative parent species disappear as derived species become established. Concentration of intermediates in older rocks, beyond a preservation null, would support the claim; frequent persistence of intermediates beside their descendants would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Parent species are rarely identifiable, and naming practices treat intermediates as separate extinct taxa.

Only a few clades have dense fossil and character data together.

Absence of intermediates is also the expected result of an incomplete rock record.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

operationalizability: 0.52
data existence: 0.66
analysis feasibility: 0.5
